name: Kulango, Nassian variety
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Micheli, Ilaria. 2017. Son of the root. Djedwa Yao Kuman, Kulango healer and hunter. Translated by Mark Brady. Trieste: EUT Edizioni Università di Trieste (ATrA – Aree di transizione linguistiche e culturali in Africa, 2). 298 pp. ISBN 978-88-8303-797-9 (online). Open access (OpenstarTs, CC).
catalog_locator: p. 13, fn. 4 (Introduction; running footer 'introduction 13'); text footnotes on verb tone: fn. 172 (p. 152), fn. 183 (p. 153), fn. 212 (p. 156), fn. 746 (p. 208), fn. 1171 (p. 254).
catalog_quote: In Kulango tone is confined to a grammatical function on verbs; it is not a lexical marker. ... For the imperatival construction (Pronoun + high tone + verb + high tone), see Micheli 2007: 78-79. ... In interrogative phrases the A tone in the second part of the negation disappears in end-phrase downdrift. See Micheli 2007: 85. ... With the exception of the first, all the verbs in the sentence have an injunctive tonal structure; see Micheli 2007: 79. ... The tonal structure with an M tone on the second morpheme of the negation -ɩ is compulsory in a negative interrogative. See Micheli 2007: 85.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: In Kulango tone is confined to a grammatical function on verbs; it is not a lexical marker.
new_statements.citation: Micheli, Ilaria & Mark Brady. 2017. Son of the root. Djedwa Yao Kuman, Kulango healer and hunter. Trieste: EUT Edizioni Università di Trieste (ATrA 2), p. 13, footnote 4.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (EUT, 298 pp., text) opened with extracted text. PDF page 13 = printed p. 13 (Introduction; running footer "introduction 13"), footnote 4 reads exactly: "In Kulango tone is confined to a grammatical function on verbs; it is not a lexical marker." The footnote hangs on "Abron tonal sounds" (the talking drums), so it is a first-hand aside by the grammar's author, not a phonology section. a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/syllable: no stress or accent statement anywhere in the book; the only other prosodic remarks are text footnotes on verb tone (imperative = pronoun + high tone + verb + high tone, Micheli 2007: 78-79; injunctive tonal structure, 2007: 79; M tone on negation…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand statement opened says Kulango is a tone language in which tone has grammatical (verbal) rather than lexical function; the same author's texts mark a high/mid/low distinction on verbs (imperative = pronoun + high tone + verb + high tone, referred to Micheli 2007: 78-79, 85). No opened source says anything about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the review of Micheli 2007 (Fiorio 2011) reports three distinctive tones, which is a slightly different characterisation from the footnote's 'not a lexical marker'.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about tone on verbs in the Nassian variety; nothing on word-level stress, citation forms or phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand statement opened (Micheli & Brady 2017) describes the Nassian variety of Kulango; Micheli 2007 and its review also cover Nassian. Glottolog files Nassian under Bondoukou Kulango (bond1246), with Bouna (Elders 2008, Prost 1974) as the separate language boun1245. Kra's Corela articles concern the Tanda dialect (also bond1246). The Fiorio 2011 review says Kulango has three dialects: Bouna (north), Bondoukou/Tanda (south-west) and Nassian.
